episode_title: Don't Mess With the Price System

stories.summary: Amit opens with a riff: as we age, gravity defeats us, we slouch, our 'body roundness index' rises. So why not use the coercive power of the state to outlaw gravity? Pass a law against it. The setup is a frame for the whole episode: gravity is to physics what supply-and-demand is to economics. You cannot legislate either away.
stories.insight: Hubris is hubris regardless of the domain. Once you accept that the state can repeal physical laws by decree, you've already conceded the logic that justifies repealing economic laws by decree. The price system is gravity for the economy.

stories.topic: The Steel and Cement Ministry's Mourning
stories.summary: A journalist friend of Ajay's covered the cement and steel ministries in the early 1980s, when their respective price controls were abolished. On the day of the announcement, the entire government building was in mourning, as if a family member had died. The market would now figure out cement and steel; the bureaucrats' importance had been knocked out overnight.
stories.insight: Price controls aren't only an economic failure mode; they are an institutional self-preservation engine. The 'aura of catastrophe' shows that the real loss to bureaucrats wasn't policy but power. In a sensible country, you don't need a ministry of steel.

stories.summary: As a college student, Amit volunteered with paramedic friends after the Latur earthquake. In a half-flattened village, the lone grocery store was charging high prices and locals were furious. Amit, then reading Marx, instinctively sided with the locals — 'evil capitalists.' Years later he saw it differently: high prices in a disaster zone are the signal that pulls in more supply and rations existing supply to those who need it most. Disaster relief is for governments to fund directly, not for the price system to absorb.
stories.insight: Bleeding-heart instincts often misdiagnose the moral landscape. The 'gouger' in a disaster is often the only one keeping anything on the shelf. Compassion that interferes with prices can starve the affected; compassion that funds purchases at high prices feeds them.

stories.topic: Friend Misses A Flight Because Of A Delhi Uber Cap
stories.summary: Delhi at one point experimented with a cap on Uber surge pricing. A friend of Amit's, who knows economic theory well enough to have predicted the shortage, still got caught out — he missed his flight because every cab was already taken. The cap converted a market that prices would have rationed (people with urgent needs pay more, casuals defer) into a brutal first-come-first-served lottery.
stories.insight: When you cap a price, you don't ration by need; you ration by luck and queue position. The person heading to the hospital and the person heading to brunch are now equal claimants on a shrinking pool — and the brunch-goer, who happened to open the app first, wins.

stories.topic: The Marine Drive Buildings That Time Forgot
stories.summary: Walk along Marine Drive in Bombay and you see grand old buildings visibly dilapidated. Why? Rent control. Tenants in some of these flats pay 150 rupees a month on units that would otherwise rent for 4-5 lakh. Owners stop maintaining; new developers stop building; the building rots; the surrounding non-controlled rents are pushed higher because supply has dried up.
stories.insight: Rent control is theft executed slowly and visibly. The decay isn't an unintended consequence — it is exactly what economic theory predicts. The buildings rot in plain sight, year after year, as a permanent monument to the policy.

stories.topic: The Statist Friend In The Rent-Controlled Flat
stories.summary: A leftist friend of Amit and Ajay's — a hardcore statist who believes the government must control everything — has lived for two generations in a rent-controlled flat near Shivaji Park. Amit notes the irony: the friend has been a lifelong personal beneficiary of state-enabled theft from a landlord while ideologically defending the state's right to do exactly that.
stories.insight: Where you stand depends on where you sit. Ideology rarely survives contact with personal incentive. The most reliable predictor of someone's politics is often what arrangement they personally happen to be benefiting from.

stories.topic: Europe Did Not Cap Gas Prices
stories.summary: When Putin cut Russian gas to Europe in 2022, prices went 'to infinity.' Russian propaganda was explicit: Europeans would freeze, then beg. What stunned Ajay was that no European policymaker reached for price caps. Instead, they let prices rise. High prices forced rationing on the demand side (factories switching fuels, shutting down, or paying through the nose by choice). High prices triggered miraculous supply: new LNG terminals built at impossible speed, tankers diverted from Qatar, US shale gas surging. For poor households, governments simply wrote checks — on-budget subsidies that let them buy expensive gas. Europe defeated Russian energy blackmail.
stories.insight: This is the textbook playbook done right. The price system handles allocation and supply response; the fiscal system handles distribution. Mix them up — by capping prices instead of cutting cheques — and you get neither supply nor relief. Europe's response is one of the most perfect public-policy stories of our era.

stories.topic: Sabudana And The Mondegreen That Wasn't
stories.summary: For years Amit misheard a line from a song in the film Gharaonda — 'Aab-daana dhoondhta hai, ashiyaana' (one searches for sustenance and shelter) — as 'Sabudana dhoondhta hai' (one searches for sago). A mondegreen. He used the song's actual theme — loneliness in the city, the search for a home — as the entry into his column on rent control.
stories.insight: Even the misheard version captures something true about cities: people arrive looking for shelter, and policy decides whether they find it. A song about loneliness and shelter is a better entry to housing economics than any equation.

stories.topic: India's Minimum Wage And The Lowest Employment Rate In The World
stories.summary: India has a minimum wage of about 13,000 rupees, while Bangladesh — a comparable economy — has 8,000. Add mandatory entitlements and the all-in cost of a formal-sector worker in India climbs to about 17,000 a month. This same number anchors NREGS welfare payments. So the policy hits both sides: firms can't afford unskilled labour (auto factories hire college grads for shop floors instead), and workers anchor on a wage they expect from welfare. Result: India has one of the world's lowest employment-to-population rates — lower than Bangladesh, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia.
stories.insight: A single policy lever, badly set, can suppress both labour demand and labour supply at once. The 'minimum wage' isn't just a floor on wages — it's a floor on dignity that has the perverse effect of pushing people out of work entirely. The alternative to a low-wage job is not a high-wage job; it's no job.

stories.summary: Punjab is arid; rice is thirsty. But the government announced a rice MSP for Punjab. Farmers responded rationally: use the free electricity to dig borewells, drain aquifers, grow rice anyway. After harvest they're stuck with rice stubble and the cheapest disposal is to burn it. Every year the foul wind from those fires becomes Delhi's worst pollution event. The same political party governs both states and still cannot fix it — the entrenched beneficiaries fight back tooth and nail.
stories.insight: Bad price interventions don't just create inefficiencies — they create political constituencies that lock the inefficiency in place. The MSP is upstream of the borewell, the borewell is upstream of the stubble, the stubble is upstream of the smog, and the smog is upstream of a political problem with no exit. One distorted price, an entire chain of catastrophe.

stories.summary: Watching how import tariffs work — domestic producers lobby for protection, the state taxes the cheaper foreign good, dispersed consumers each pay a few rupees extra without noticing, the aggregate goes to the protected industry — Amit named what he saw: 'Every interference in free markets leads to a redistribution of wealth from the poor to the rich.' The poor consumers' rupees, scattered and invisible, get gathered up and handed to a politically organised producer interest.
stories.insight: The structure of every protectionist policy is the same: visible concentrated benefit, invisible dispersed cost. Public-choice mechanics ensure the concentrated beneficiaries lobby and the dispersed losers don't. So the well-intended intervention becomes a regressive transfer by default.

stories.topic: Azar Nafisi On Where To Find Liberalism
stories.summary: At a liberalism conference in DC, Amit heard Azar Nafisi (Reading Lolita in Tehran) say something he can't shake: if you want to hear classical liberal values expressed in their truest sense, listen to the dissenters in Iran. For them it is existential — they take nothing for granted. In America, freedoms have been guaranteed so long that people can spend their politics on luxury beliefs without ever defending the foundations.
stories.insight: Liberty is a muscle that atrophies without use. The places where liberal values are spoken most clearly are the places where they are most under threat. Comfort is the slow erosion of vocabulary. A young Indian born in 2004 has no living memory of pre-liberalisation India; the lessons are fading even where the wounds were freshest.

recommendations.item: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on four foundational economics papers, including Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society.'
recommendations.reason: The deeper backstory for this episode's central claim — that prices coordinate dispersed knowledge no central planner could ever assemble. Hayek's 1940s essay against central planning is the source code.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's 1945 essay arguing that the price system is a decentralised information system that no central planner can replicate.
recommendations.reason: The single most important paper for understanding why markets work. Amit returns to it again and again because the insight — that prices aggregate millions of pieces of dispersed local knowledge — is the foundation of every argument in this episode.

recommendations.item: The Fatal Conceit
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's late book naming the central planner's fundamental error.
recommendations.reason: The 'fatal conceit' is the belief that one mind, or one committee, could ever know enough to design society from the top down. The very title is a permanent rebuke to every well-intentioned price control.

recommendations.item: I, Pencil
recommendations.creator: Leonard Read
recommendations.context: Read's classic 1958 essay told from the perspective of a pencil describing how no single human could make it.
recommendations.reason: The most accessible, almost devotional account of spontaneous order. A pencil involves the cooperation of millions of people across forty countries — none of whom know each other, and none of whom needed to. Prices alone made it happen.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column using a thought experiment — a 10,000-rupee price cap on cars — to show what price caps actually do.
recommendations.reason: The piece that gives this episode its argumentative spine. Caps don't lower prices; they make goods disappear, generate shortages, and eventually push activity into black markets.

recommendations.item: Prices, Fast and Slow
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's NIPFP paper on price flexibility and the political economy of allowing prices to move.
recommendations.reason: Amit's pick of the day. He wanted to discuss it during the episode but it didn't fit the narrative — so he sends listeners directly to the source. A deeper treatment of when prices are allowed to do their work and when they aren't.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's long-form Seen and the Unseen episode on the war.
recommendations.reason: The broader context for this episode's Europe-and-gas story — what blackmail looked like, why Europe was vulnerable, and how it pulled itself out.

recommendations.item: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on the war.
recommendations.reason: Companion piece to the deep-dive — the EIE-format treatment of how the war evolved and what was at stake.

recommendations.item: Russia, Ukraine, Foreign Policy (Episode 268 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai
recommendations.context: Amit's early-war episode with the Takshashila Institution founders.
recommendations.reason: Recorded just after the invasion. Pranay and Nitin warned that Europe's gas dependence on Russia was about to become blackmail material. The episode is the receipt — the prediction was right.

recommendations.item: The Complete Yes Minister
recommendations.creator: Antony Jay and Jonathan Lynn
recommendations.context: The book of the British political comedy series.
recommendations.reason: Source of the line that explains every bad policy: 'This is a problem, we must do something. This is something. Let's do it.' That sentence is the entire psychology behind price caps, rent controls, and minimum wages.

recommendations.item: Alone in the City
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Houseful Economics column using the Gharaonda song to discuss rent control and the search for shelter in cities.
recommendations.reason: The piece that connects the loneliness of urban life to the housing policies that make cities harder to enter. A more humane way into a topic usually argued in graphs.

recommendations.item: Rent Control (Episode 14 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
recommendations.context: An early Seen and Unseen episode where the economist Alex Tabarrok explained New York's rent-control devastation.
recommendations.reason: Source of the image Amit keeps returning to: rent-controlled parts of New York looked like a 'bombed out city,' so dystopian that movies like Escape from New York were set in them. A vivid case study of what price ceilings on housing actually produce.

recommendations.item: San Fransicko
recommendations.creator: Michael Shellenberger
recommendations.context: Shellenberger's account of progressive policy failure in San Francisco.
recommendations.reason: Modern proof that the rent-control mistake hasn't been learned. Among many factors, well-intentioned price controls helped make one of America's wealthiest cities unaffordable to the people the controls were meant to help.

recommendations.item: The Mystery of Capital
recommendations.creator: Hernando de Soto
recommendations.context: De Soto's classic on property rights and 'dead capital' in the developing world.
recommendations.reason: Frames rent control as a form of theft — and shows what happens when secure property rights are absent. Capital that can't be transacted, owned, or improved upon stops working as capital at all.

recommendations.item: Milton Friedman on the Minimum Wage
recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Friedman's famous explanation, on video, of why minimum wage laws cause unemployment.
recommendations.reason: The clip that changed Amit's mind on minimum wage. He once supported it; watching Friedman's argument tipped him into the rabbit hole of books that rebuilt his worldview. Worth seven minutes of anyone's life.

recommendations.item: Illiberal Reformers
recommendations.creator: Thomas Leonard
recommendations.context: Leonard's history of the Progressive-era American economists who designed minimum-wage laws.
recommendations.reason: The uncomfortable origin story. Many early-20th-century minimum wage laws were explicitly designed by their authors to keep African-Americans, immigrants, and women out of the labour force. The privileged protecting themselves, dressed up as compassion.

recommendations.item: Understanding India's Pensions Disaster (Episode 65 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's previous episode on the unraveling of Indian pension reform.
recommendations.reason: Cited as evidence of the same generational-amnesia problem: 25 years after the original pensions reform, the lessons have been forgotten and the mistakes are returning.

recommendations.item: Snatching decline from the jaws of growth
recommendations.creator: KP Krishnan
recommendations.context: Krishnan's Business Standard column on how to break the political logjam on Indian labour law.
recommendations.reason: The clever proposal Ajay endorses: start labour-law deregulation in IT and IT-enabled services, where the workers are clearly competent adults who don't need state paternalism, and expand outward as the experiment proves itself.

recommendations.item: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Episode 46 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on Rob Henderson's concept of 'luxury beliefs.'
recommendations.reason: Frames the minimum wage and other interventions as luxury beliefs — virtue-signalling positions held by people whose lives are not affected by the consequences. The position feels good; the policy harms the very people it claims to help.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Episode 57 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on what actually drives human development.
recommendations.reason: The argument Amit references for why economic freedom is upstream of every welfare indicator. You don't get health, education, or longevity outcomes by ordering them — you get them by allowing growth, which requires freedom, which requires not interfering with prices.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's deep dive on Indian agricultural policy.
recommendations.reason: The longer treatment of MSPs, the carbohydrate-vs-protein epidemic they helped seed in the 1960s, and the cascade from rice MSPs in Punjab to Delhi's smog. Worth the full episode for anyone who wants the receipts.

recommendations.item: The Great Redistribution
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on how state interventions redistribute wealth in unexpected directions.
recommendations.reason: The fuller statement of Verma's Law — that nearly every interference with free markets transfers wealth from dispersed poor consumers to organised rich producers.

recommendations.item: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on Indian firms competing internationally.
recommendations.reason: The long-form argument for why exposure to international competition forces firms to lift their game, why tariffs hide the deficiency, and why Indian firms that compete globally end up better at everything.

recommendations.item: Reading Lolita in Tehran
recommendations.creator: Azar Nafisi
recommendations.context: Nafisi's memoir of teaching Western literature in post-revolutionary Iran.
recommendations.reason: Cited not just for itself but for Nafisi's living point — that classical liberal values are spoken most clearly by those who have lost them. People in comfortable democracies have forgotten the vocabulary the dissenters in Iran still need every day.

recommendations.item: Slouching Towards Utopia
recommendations.creator: Brad DeLong
recommendations.context: DeLong's economic history of the 20th century.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's pick for understanding the post-1989 economic-policy consensus — the one that has now fragmented under Trump, Putin, Xi, and the rise of right-wing authoritarianism. To know what we are losing, read what we had.

recommendations.item: Price Theory
recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Friedman's classic microeconomics textbook from his University of Chicago lectures.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's beautiful book from his childhood. Sometimes the old masters got it right and we should just go back. The clearest exposition of how prices actually work.

core_ideas.concept: Resource Allocation As The Hidden Document
core_ideas.explanation: Imagine writing down a complete specification of every productive activity in an economy: who cuts which tree, who transports it, who runs the lumber mill, who makes the pencil. That document — millions of pages long — is what economists call 'the resource allocation.' Central planning is the dream that a government can write this document. Markets are the alternative: millions of independent decision-makers, each pursuing self-interest, with prices being the only thing that crosses the cell wall of any one firm — and somehow that single signal is enough to discover the entire document.
core_ideas.quote: The price system discovers the resource allocation, and it does a darn good job.

core_ideas.explanation: Every price does two jobs at once. As information, it tells producers and consumers something about the world they couldn't otherwise know — a fire destroys 10% of India's timber and the price of pencils nudges up. As incentive, it pulls behaviour in productive directions — the higher pencil price draws new entrants, substitute hunters, and economisers. Both functions break the moment you cap the price. Capping it is like silencing the radio in a storm.
core_ideas.quote: Prices act as both information and they act as incentives.

core_ideas.explanation: When 200 Ubers meet 200 riders, the market clears. When supply halves to 100 cabs, surge pricing kicks in: the price rises until the people who most need a ride (hospital, airport) outbid the people who casually wanted one (errand, brunch). Simultaneously, idle drivers see the surge and join the supply. Within minutes prices fall back. Cap the surge and you destroy both functions at once: rationing collapses to first-come-first-served (lottery), and supply doesn't expand. The friend who missed his flight is the demonstration.
core_ideas.quote: Those are not numbers. Those are people talking to each other.

core_ideas.explanation: Putin's energy blackmail in 2022 was supposed to break Europe. The European response was a textbook of how to do public policy: (1) let the price go to infinity, so demand rationed itself onto its highest-value uses; (2) trust that the high price would generate supply — and it did, with new LNG terminals built at impossible speed, tankers diverted from Qatar, US shale surging into European ports; (3) protect the poor on-budget, by writing them cheques to buy expensive gas — never by capping the gas price itself. The price system did allocation; the fiscal system did distribution. Each tool to its proper job.
core_ideas.quote: This is just one of the most perfect stories of how to do public policy.

core_ideas.explanation: Every interference with the free market redistributes wealth from the poor to the rich. The mechanism is always the same: dispersed costs on many consumers (each barely noticing), concentrated benefits to a few politically organised producers (each lobbying hard). Tariffs, MSPs, quotas, licenses — all share this signature. The intuition that intervention helps the weak is almost always inverted.
core_ideas.quote: Every interference in free markets leads to a redistribution of wealth from the poor to the rich.

core_ideas.explanation: Cap the rent and three things follow. The landlord stops maintaining the building (no return on the investment), so the asset rots. New developers stop building in the area (no point), so housing supply contracts. Outside the controlled zone, prices spike (the controlled supply is locked up). The visible beneficiary — the long-term tenant — gains; the invisible victims — every other renter, every would-be tenant, the city itself — lose. The Marine Drive landlord paid 150 rupees a month forever is the stolen-from party; he is the one being expropriated, slowly, year by year.

Labour laws are sold as protections for workers. Their mechanism is to ban certain employment contracts — specifically, the low-wage contracts available to people whose work isn't (yet) worth the floor. The result: those people don't get protected; they get unemployed. India's minimum wage and entitlement stack drives all-in formal labour costs above market-clearing levels, and the country's employment-to-population rate is among the world's lowest — below Bangladesh, below Pakistan, below Saudi Arabia. The same coalition of leftists, left economists, and policymakers that claims to be pro-worker is, in effect, the anti-worker coalition.
core_ideas.quote: The alternative to a low-wage job is not a high-wage job. The alternative to a low-wage job is no job.

core_ideas.explanation: Hayek and Friedman won the argument a generation ago. The result was decades of prosperity. But prosperity creates a problem: the people enjoying it inherit the institutions without inheriting the reasons. Like the sorcerer's apprentice, they know which spell makes the broom carry water, but not why — and so they tweak it, intervene, mess with prices, expecting the broom to keep working. Every 20 or 30 years governments must be allowed to fail visibly so the lesson can be relearned. Otherwise interventionism returns by default.
core_ideas.quote: Every generation has to fight its own battles.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's compressed definition of political maturity: the ability to stomach large prices. Wisdom is creating a world of freedom where prices fluctuate, then doing nothing with state power when they do. The fluctuation isn't a problem — it is the sound of the resource allocation refashioning itself in response to a war, a drought, a discovery. Shut off that sound and you stop the rebuilding. The mature government writes a cheque to the poor and lets the price do its work.
core_ideas.quote: The fluctuating of prices is the sound of the resource allocation getting refashioned.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's working definition: a leftist is not someone who cares about people. A leftist is someone who wants to use state coercion to refashion society. The two are opposites. Caring about people requires respecting their autonomy and reasoning carefully about consequences; coercion shortcuts both. Many policies that sound compassionate — minimum wage, rent control, MSPs — are not compassionate at all once you trace their effects. They are violence with a virtuous brand.
core_ideas.quote: True compassion has to be centered on a respect for individual autonomy and individual freedom.

core_ideas.explanation: The political logjam on labour reform feels unbreakable because every reform proposal is met with the paternalist objection that workers can't fend for themselves. KP Krishnan's wedge: start where that objection collapses on its own. Indian IT and ITeS workers are demonstrably capable adults who can change jobs the next day if mistreated. Pick a state, deregulate labour law in IT/ITeS only, see what happens. If it works, expand to garments, toys, low-end electronics. Reform doesn't have to be all-or-nothing; it can be the slow widening of an already-proven crack.

A tariff doesn't just transfer money from consumers to a domestic producer. It removes the discipline that forces the producer to improve. Without competition, there's no incentive to lift game on price or quality. Indian firms exposed to international competition routinely become world-class — because they have to. The tariff insulates a firm from the very pressure that would have made it good. Protection is a slow-acting toxin disguised as nourishment.

A single distorted price compounds outward. Rice MSP creates incentive to grow rice in arid Punjab. Free agricultural electricity makes borewell-pumping free. Aquifers drain. After harvest, stubble accumulates. The cheapest disposal is fire. The smoke drifts to Delhi every autumn. The political cost of unwinding any link is too high — the same party governs both states and still cannot fix it. One bad price intervention has manufactured an entrenched political constituency around its own continuation. This is why bad policies are so much harder to remove than to install.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening proposal: gravity is the cause of slouching and aging, so the state should outlaw gravity. He even asks Ajay to write the application in triplicate.
Ajay's offered title for the resulting bestseller: 'Floating to Utopia: The Gorgeous Economics of Outlawing Gravity.'

Amit on consenting-adult freedom: 'There will be one group of people who will be like, two consenting adults can do whatever they want in the bedroom, but not in the marketplace. And another group which will say the opposite thing. And it doesn't make sense. Freedom is freedom.'
Amit on bureaucratic mourning: when the price control on cement and steel was abolished, the entire ministry building had 'an aura of catastrophe like some family member has died.'
Amit on the leftist friend in the rent-controlled flat: 'Where you stand depends on where you sit. He has been a lifelong beneficiary of theft enabled by the state.'
Amit's mondegreen: hearing 'Aab-daana dhoondhta hai' (one searches for sustenance) as 'Sabudana dhoondhta hai' (one searches for sago). 'Full starch, by the way.'
Amit on tariffs: 'I don't know how you feel about this matter. I hate tariffs. I fucking hate import tariffs.'
Ajay on the Bengali soul: 'Slouching towards utopia totally embodies all Bengaliness. Slouching is a physical surrender; the irrational desire for utopia is the intellectual.'
Amit's redefinition: 'Every party in India is left wing on economics, every party is right wing on society. They are anti-freedom on every margin.'
Amit on body roundness: noting Ajay introduced him to the 'body roundness index' a day or two ago — 'I think only to be able to cast a slur upon me without sounding rude.'
Yes Minister: 'This is a problem. We must do something. This is something. Let's do it.' The standard line behind every reflexive price intervention.
Friedrich Hayek's 'fatal conceit' — the belief that a single planner could ever know enough to design society from the top down.
Leonard Read's I, Pencil — no single human can make a pencil; cooperation across forty countries does it through prices alone.
Nixon's 1970s gasoline price cap during the OPEC crisis, producing the famous photographs of long American queues at gas stations.
Venezuela's regime price controls and the resulting black-market queues for toilet paper and milk.
Soviet bread rationing and the food lines that wrapped around city blocks.
John Carpenter's Escape from New York — set in a dystopian rent-control-blighted New York, cited by Alex Tabarrok as what parts of the city actually felt like.
Roosevelt instituting rent control in New York in the 1940s — the original American sin that India copied from 1949 onward.
Hernando de Soto's concept of 'dead capital' — assets that can't be transacted, owned, or improved upon, so they stop functioning as capital.
Angela Merkel: we will only know the future of Germany when the generations with no memory of the Second World War come of age and develop their own political philosophy.
George Santayana: 'Those who fail to learn from history are doomed to repeat it' — invoked as the closing frame for this episode's argument about generational amnesia.
Bob Dylan: 'He not busy being born is busy dying' — Amit's quote when introducing Life Lessons, on why learning has to be continuous.
'OECD hote hobe' — Amit's mock-Bengali for 'we must become OECD,' the political ambition behind the absurd 10,000-rupee car price cap thought experiment.
